status: design research only. No runtime results.

scope.method: All current MDX and referenced YAML sources read by extraction scripts; phase/activity/reference structure and exact result declarations inventoried. Task/result/recall/epilogue content and relevant fixtures reviewed for design. This does not execute examples, prove capture reachability, audit every nested reference, renew the whole-course pedagogical audit, or report learner validation.

globalRules: Current output is evidence only if its capture was reached; declaration presence does not imply availability after a failure.
Keep measured output, supplied input, authored scene, and external self-report distinct.

Never infer semantics from an arbitrary title or slug alone, and never parse summary prose. An exact frozen title plus column schema may identify a role only within a verified exercise and fixture-version contract.
A submission may contain different probes, candidates, or model states. Explicit compatibility is required for linked selections.
Some different checks share state intentionally; gradient-step and export-model-artifact require authored continuity, not automatic isolation.
Keep the whole relevant bounded case set; excerpts disclose selected and total counts.
Inspecting or saving a result adds no lesson credit and triggers no automatic rerun.
Do not create a full spectrogram, loss curve, gate trace, or attention explanation from absent operands.
Retain existing recall tasks and delayed answer reveals; result anchors must not supply graded answers before an attempt.
Keep authored epilogues visible and preserve story decision consequences independently of result inspection.
Each entry inherits its lesson source boundary and limits, plus these global rules. A captureCheck names source code, not a current typed result group.
Default to transient current-run results. Saving outside the existing data/network/evaluation stages requires a later explicit retention decision.
globalDependencies: versioned result definition with explicit artifact roles and reviewed compatibility
independent check, result availability, interpretation, and assistance states

tensor-layout: array order and explicit sensor/time axes
calculation: the lesson-specific operation before interpreting output
training-history: training versus validation versus final evaluation
model state and recorded epoch identity
classification-cases: score versus label versus decision rule
evaluation set membership and error categories

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: The LSTM misses a warning ripple near the start of an 80-step window. Farah tries attention so the forecast can read earlier hidden states directly.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Attention compares a query with keys, then uses the resulting weights to combine values. A higher weight gives a value more influence in the blend. It does not prove that input caused the prediction.
recallQuestions: What do the query, keys, and values each do?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The attention weights highlight two parts of the eighty-step window. The crew checks those readings and tests the forecasts on separate sequences.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Let a forecast read earlier hidden states. The exercise uses fixed synthetic query/keys and twice-identity values as a weight-revealing probe.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: The probe performs no training and explains no forecast. Do not claim attention weights prove causal importance. Key width and value width can differ.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Demir applies attention across time. The model gives each step in a signal window a weight, then combines the readings using those weights.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Temporal attention gives each time step a weight, then blends its values into a summary. A larger weight gives that step more influence in the blend. Its value also matters, so the weight alone cannot explain a prediction.
recallQuestions: What can an attention plot tell you, and what does it leave uncertain?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The largest attention weights fall near the amplitude spike and a frequency shift 74 readings later. The crew checks the timestamps too. The weights alone do not confirm a physical pattern.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Blend readings with a scorer that can consider position. The current output uses three synthetic readings and a supplied position-only scorer.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: The added position column helps calculate scores but must stay out of the summary. Weights alone establish neither cause nor anomaly. Preserve the [1] feature axis for one-feature cases.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: The crew needs to know when the anomaly will return. Demir builds a model that uses past readings to forecast what comes next.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Forecasting uses past readings to predict future values. If each prediction becomes the next input, an error can affect later predictions too. That does not mean the error grows at every step.
recallQuestions: Why can errors build up when a forecast reuses its own predictions, even if the data pattern stays the same?
Error triples between short and long horizons of one rollout. What comparison did you make?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The forecast predicts the anomaly will repeat at a specific time. It does not. The signal's timing is changing, and not randomly.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Compare forecasts that use previous predictions with replays that receive later observations. The current exercise trains once on a synthetic scalar series.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: Do not assume either method must win or errors must grow monotonically. This scalar fixture is separate from the previous module’s three-feature forecaster. The story’s failed schedule remains a crew event.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: The time between pulses keeps changing. Demir tries a moving average to smooth the noisy measurements, but the smoothed value falls behind the change.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: A Kalman filter predicts a value, then updates it when a new measurement arrives. It calculates how much weight to give the prediction and the measurement from their uncertainty.
recallQuestions: Consider the scalar update: estimate = prediction + gain × (measurement − prediction).
Why can a one-state level filter lag behind steadily falling measurements?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The log shows the gap between pulses shrinking by about a sixth of a second per day. The Kalman estimate is smoother, but trails the latest measurement by about 0.43 seconds.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Follow changing pulse intervals without hiding lag. The exercise returns actual filter estimates for a fictional eight-day first-cycle log.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: The one-state filter models a level, not a changing rate. Smoothness establishes no accuracy gain. Day 1 initializes the filter and must not appear as an observed update.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: No single model handles all aspects of the signal. Demir combines the LSTM, attention model, and Kalman filter into an ensemble: multiple models, one prediction.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: An ensemble runs several models on the same input and combines their predictions. Some errors can cancel each other. Mistakes shared by all the models stay in the combined result.
recallQuestions: When does combining models help, and how should you check?
An ensemble has MAE 0.041. Its members have 0.052, 0.036 and 0.050. Did it beat the best member?
Why can raw sensor counts and radians give unbalanced weights when we combine their errors?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The blend beats its best single member on the held-out week, 0.036 against 0.038. Demir keeps all three models and still fits the compression line by hand.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Check whether blending actually improves on the best member. Current output compares member and blend MAE on four synthetic targets.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: Prior held-out errors set weights on their own normalized scale. Current-window MAE uses arbitrary target units. Neither weighted blending nor the story’s 0.036 score guarantees a gain on another period.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: DEEP SCAN flags a signal that doesn't match any known category. Nazari challenges: is the model broken, or have they found something new?
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Anomaly detection learns what normal readings look like, then flags readings that differ. You cannot list every possible anomaly in advance. Build a baseline from reviewed normal readings, then check it on separate data.
recallQuestions: At a 0.27% false-alarm rate and 100,000 normal readings per hour, about how many flags occur per hour?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The crew needs to define what a normal reading looks like before deciding which readings to flag. Demir starts with the readings they have already checked.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Define normal before flagging readings. The primary probe uses a synthetic baseline. The incident uses recent synthetic rows supplied as human-reviewed normal.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: A flag does not identify a cause. The candidate baseline currently fits and checks the same rows. Preserve the unknown truth of sample 7741 and optional training-set decision.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Simple statistics miss complex patterns. Farah proposes an autoencoder: a network that learns to compress and reconstruct normal signals. High reconstruction error gives the crew a reason to investigate. They still need to find its cause.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: An autoencoder learns to compress and rebuild its training data. Reconstruction error can help flag unusual inputs, but it can also miss anomalies or flag normal inputs.
recallQuestions: Can an autoencoder trained on normal data also reconstruct an anomaly well?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Normal signals come back clean. The anomalous signal comes back at 1.4x baseline, below the cutoff used in this run. The crew finds suspect rows in training and investigates whether they contributed to the miss.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Train only on rows allowed into the normal baseline and inspect reconstructions. Current output measures MSE on separate synthetic eight-feature inputs.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: Actual stochastic scores must replace no fictional ratio. Current artifact is aggregate, so per-feature reconstruction needs extra capture. Flagged-row exclusion alone does not prove a representative clean baseline.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Demir feeds the anomalous signal through the autoencoder. The reconstruction differs sharply from the input. The error is 12x the normal maximum. Farah: 'That is our anomaly score.'
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Reconstruction error measures the difference between an input and the autoencoder's rebuilt version. It gives one score per input. A high score means the model rebuilt it poorly.
recallQuestions: What can the total reconstruction error tell you, and what needs a separate feature-by-feature check?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The error is twelve times the highest normal error. Most comes from fft_5, the bin centered at 72 Hz, nearest to the 73.4 Hz component.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Measure mismatch between an input and its reconstruction, then investigate a missed confirmed event. The primary probe uses a synthetic offset model. The incident supplies per-feature baselines.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: Do not substitute the incident’s absolute errors for the primary task’s MSE. The story’s twelve-times-normal case remains separate. Neither ratio nor error proves the cause of a missed event.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Nazari demands precise thresholds. 'If DEEP SCAN cries wolf one more time, the bridge crew will ignore it. Set the sensitivity correctly.'
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: The threshold decides which readings trigger an alert. Set it too low and the crew gets too many false alarms. Set it too high and the detector misses more anomalies.
recallQuestions: What does F1 measure, and when might you choose a different cutoff?
Why might a detector that saves captures need a different cutoff from one that wakes the crew?
A threshold at the 99th percentile leaves about 1% of the sampled normal errors above it.
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Demir checks how many alerts the crew would receive: a 1% false-alarm rate means about 26 a day on this archive. He chooses a cutoff of 1.0 and records how many anomalies it misses. None of the normal validation readings crosses it.

referenceInventory.summary: Optional: compare threshold policies on held-out cases

lessons.sourceBoundary: Balance missed events against crew review load. Current threshold result uses six synthetic labeled cases. A separate incident supplies alert counts and a sensor-change log.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: Threshold selection uses validation data, with strictly greater-than flagging and allowed tied winners. Six cases establish no future alert rate or deployment optimum. Preserve separate story archive counts and cost assumptions.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: The crew replays sample 7741, a reading marked normal during the quiet period. Then a live capture shows the same pattern, with twelve times the highest reconstruction error seen on normal readings.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: An ensemble combines several detectors. Its alert counts how many checks flagged a reading. That count helps the crew decide what to investigate, but it does not prove the signal is new or explain its cause.
recallQuestions: The amplitude check stays quiet, but the autoencoder and LSTM both flag a reading. What should the 2-of-3 ensemble report, and what does that result mean?
Why does the sensor's maximum reading limit how large this amplitude z-score can get?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Fibonacci ratios, the same sequence the ship's own sensor calibration uses. Farah runs the decomposition again. Same ratios.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Combine independent checks on the latest reading for investigation. The probe calculates a statistical vote but receives reconstruction and forecast scores as supplied inputs.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: This exercise does not execute an autoencoder or LSTM. Votes are not probabilities. The Fibonacci/calibration discovery is a fixed crew record and does not establish the signal’s source.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Nazari wants the classifier on the bridge dashboard, where the crew can use it. The dashboard must process each reading locally.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Running predictions in the browser can keep each input on the device. The device still needs the model, runtime, enough memory and processing power. Offline use needs a caching plan, and other parts of the app may still upload data.
recallQuestions: What tradeoff comes with moving inference into the browser?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Nazari approves the browser deployment plan. Demir begins setting up the runtime.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Choose where dashboard inference can meet privacy, offline, size, and latency requirements. Current output evaluates supplied policy boundary cases.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: These rules are authored policy, not measured device behavior. Local inference alone does not establish that the whole application preserves privacy or works offline.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Demir begins wiring TensorFlow.js into the ship's dashboard. Nazari watches over his shoulder, timing every step.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Add TensorFlow.js as an npm dependency, then wait for it to start. Check which backend, the engine that runs its calculations, is actually available.
recallQuestions: How do you check which backend is running and whether it is fast enough?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Demir checks the backend at every station. One console uses a different backend, and Nazari asks him to record it.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Initialize the runtime for Nazari’s consoles. Current artifact reports a simulated startup with test backend names/version.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: Do not show the mock backend as the learner device’s backend. Real-device capture requires an explicit lab execution, initialization failures, and version/source metadata.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Demir tries to load the trained model into the dashboard and gets a 404 error. This model needs a JSON file and the weight files it points to.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Load the model's manifest and weight files, then inspect the input and output shapes the dashboard must use.
recallQuestions: What does tf.loadLayersModel() resolve to?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Demir loads the model and saves a copy in IndexedDB. Later, the notebook and dashboard give different scores for the same reading. He needs to check which model version each one loaded.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Recover from missing model files and inspect the model’s contract. The exercise uses a simulated loader response.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: No bridge model downloads here. The shape contract needs provenance from the loaded fixture, and this metadata output does not prove cache persistence or model-version parity.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Demir has loaded the model. He wires it into the dashboard's real-time signal feed: every second, a new reading arrives and the model must classify it.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Each reading arrives, the model makes a prediction, and the dashboard updates. Your code must also release each temporary tensor when it is no longer needed.
recallQuestions: Which tensors must you release when making repeated predictions?
At 03:00 there are 400 tensors. At 05:00 there are 1,000. The budget is 10,000.
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Green for normal, amber for anomalous: live classifications stream across the dashboard while the crew watches.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Prepare each raw reading for inference and keep temporary tensors bounded. The primary probe echoes scaled inputs. The incident uses supplied 400-to-520 tensor snapshots.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: The echo probe checks preprocessing, not classifier accuracy. Equal tensor counts are a local lifecycle check, not total browser-memory evidence. The incident can estimate headroom without identifying a leak.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Nazari asks for a comparison before the crew commits to a runtime. Demir has a model file and a laptop. She wants results from the bridge consoles.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: ONNX stores a model’s operations, connections and weights. A runtime can run the model only if it supports the operations and format version the file uses.
recallQuestions: WASM runs a small classifier faster on your laptop. What can you conclude?
What should you check before shipping an ONNX model on a new runtime?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Demir brings parity results and timings from each console. Nazari keeps TF.js for this release and files the ONNX export beside the benchmark.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Compare parity and completed prediction times before selecting a runtime. The exercise simulates ONNX and its clock.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: These simulated times rank no real runtime. Keep model loading outside the measured interval, await output readback, and separate parity from task accuracy and physical-device support.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: The bridge wants positive or negative labels on the crew’s daily status reports. After three modules of training models, Demir asks whether he needs to train another one for this job.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Transformers.js ships pretrained Hugging Face models that run in the browser. Use an existing model when its task, license and measured behavior fit your application.
recallQuestions: When is a supported pretrained Transformers.js model a reasonable starting point?
Describe how you would select and label twenty reports for an honest first evaluation of a pretrained pipeline.
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The pretrained classifier is running. Farah returns to the Sector 7-G readings in the lab.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Label the crew’s status reports with a supplied pretrained-task interface. The exercise simulates the pipeline loader and classifier.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: Fixture sentiment scores are neither real model measurements nor report urgency. Any real model execution needs a separately labeled lab, model/license revision, download state, and supported browser path.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Mirza calls the final briefing. 'Assemble the pieces into one production system, Ensign, and show me the architecture.' Demir lays out DEEP SCAN.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: The crew must connect the components from the last ten modules on one memory-limited dashboard. Each handoff needs compatible data, and each retained tensor needs an owner.
recallQuestions: Beyond package versions, what must remain compatible between ML pipeline stages?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Five components on the main display: preprocessing, feature extraction, classification, anomaly detection, reporting. Behind them the ticker reads 47.0 seconds. Mirza looks at the number, then at the five boxes that have fourteen days to be ready, and says nothing at all.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Connect DEEP SCAN’s stages under dashboard memory limits. The exercise awaits normalization, FFT, and tensor creation on an eight-sample probe.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: The any-typed stage list does not guarantee compatible TypeScript types. Runtime validators carry that responsibility. The probe’s scaler differs from the production classifier and cannot prove full-system integration.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Demir brings a green build to Nazari. The log reveals that it tested an older model than the one he intends to release.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Model releases need checks for both learned behavior and artifact identity. Test the exact graph, weights and preprocessing that the application will use.
recallQuestions: How would you check that a passing CI run tested the exact model you plan to release?
What evidence establishes that a rollback restored the intended release?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The pipeline goes green twice: once on the wrong model, once on the right one. Only the second one counts, and Nazari logs the difference in hours.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Ensure CI checks the exact candidate. One activity gates supplied labeled predictions. Another serializes and reloads a real small model in memory.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: An accuracy gate on supplied rows proves no wider performance. Round-trip parity proves neither task accuracy nor hosted deployment. The current inventory lacks release fingerprints, preprocessing, and label metadata.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: ARIA flags a concern: 'Deployment is not the end. Model performance can change as inputs and their relationship to labels change. We must watch.' Demir builds the monitoring dashboard.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: ML monitoring watches changes that may not throw an error: model scores, prediction times, and inputs that differ from the training data. These changes tell you what to investigate.
recallQuestions: What model failure can occur while latency and exception rates look normal?
How would you investigate a drift alert before the recent predictions have trusted labels?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Confidence scores, inference latency, drift detection, all streaming in real time. ARIA: 'Now we have signals to investigate. They do not establish accuracy.'

lessons.sourceBoundary: Give the watch signals to investigate after deployment. Current output calculates a synthetic mean shift and percentiles from 100 supplied durations.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: No browser timings occur in the supplied duration log. Scores are not proven calibrated probabilities. Mean shift is neither all distribution drift nor accuracy. Current unlabeled monitoring cannot authorize retraining or a model swap.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Farah asks who can operate DEEP SCAN when Demir is off watch. He starts a handover covering the model's evidence, limitations, and the decisions the next watch will face.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: ML system documentation covers the usual ground (API reference, architecture, getting started) plus the model-specific record: training data, performance characteristics, and known limitations.
recallQuestions: What evidence should accompany a measured model score?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Demir writes a Model Card, API reference, and runbook for the next operator. ARIA reviews them and asks for a missing threshold.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Prepare a handover for whoever takes the next watch. The learner renders supplied fictional metadata as a model card.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: Formatting a card does not verify its figures or establish provenance. Do not attach another lesson’s model artifact automatically. A future linked card needs explicit compatible versions and reviewed sources.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: The crew has one live pulse to check DEEP SCAN on a bridge console before expanding the release. Mirza waits for the verdict.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: A browser-only ML application can ship to a static host with its model assets. Verify the served files and behavior, and configure any required server services separately.
recallQuestions: What must you restore and check when rolling back a deployed model?
What does a two-out-of-three detector vote tell you?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: DEEP SCAN goes live. It classifies the anomalous signal. The result appears on every display on the bridge.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Apply a release policy to bounded rehearsal evidence, verify local checks, then interpret the supplied zero-hour fictional detector record. The external room-occupancy project is an independent task.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: None of the three code exercises deploys the full mission system. The two supplied 7741 scores come from different systems and imply no accuracy gain. Preserve the fixed 0157 canary, counterfactual simulations, unresolved source, and final operator_note: none. External learner performance requires inspected work, not course test completion.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: The research ship Archimedes has received an unfamiliar signal from Sector 7-G, a region of space the crew is monitoring. Its existing software, ARIA, follows rules written in advance. The crew needs to find patterns those rules have missed.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Turn Demir’s selected readings into a tensor so the supplied code can draw one line per sensor.
recallQuestions: Demir creates a tensor from the 12 selected readings.
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Demir can now follow the readings on the chart. Farah checks the code that keeps each sensor’s readings together.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Connect Demir’s selected recording to his chart. The fictional header names sensors A, B, C, D at three moments, with the same 12 values used next lesson.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: The learner creates the tensor and reads its shape. Supplied code groups and plots it. This performs no training or pattern discovery.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Demir’s chart shows a line for each selected sensor. Farah checks the code behind it to make sure each line uses the right readings.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: A grid's shape gives its number of rows and columns. Knowing what those rows and columns mean helps you arrange readings correctly.
recallQuestions: Farah checks another short list from Demir's recording: the first three sensors at two more moments. The notes label them A, B, and C, in that order each time. The list is [6, 10, 14, 7, 12, 13].
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Farah arranges Demir's full recording by sensor. The repeating waves are easier to follow on her chart.

referenceInventory.summary: Optional: images, extra axes, and memory

lessons.sourceBoundary: Keep each sensor’s readings in time order while Farah checks Demir’s same 12-value recording.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: Shape cannot establish sensor identity. Keep the authored header and value order visible. Preserve the existing prediction requirement and later full-recording story as a separate crew action.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Demir's first attempt at combining the feeds just crashed the console. Nazari needs it fixed before more readings arrive.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Add or multiply values at matching positions, or use matrix multiplication to combine them into weighted sums.
recallQuestions: Check both the dimensions and the meaning of a matrix multiplication.
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Nazari spots the same ripple repeating in an hour of combined sensor readings.

referenceInventory.summary: Reference: the original amplifier and matrix products

lessons.sourceBoundary: Repair the failed merge of two sensor passes, then mix channels. Current recorded probes use small supplied passes and a three-bank matrix.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: The recorded probes do not process the full 64-channel capture. Matrix mixing and element-wise operations need separate axis labels and explanations.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Ensign Demir needs to read the sensor archive without filling the computer's memory.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Prepare input shapes, batches and splits for the task. Shuffle training examples only when their order is not part of the example.
recallQuestions: You have chosen the training split. Now prepare its rows for mini-batch training.
Does reading one row at a time make a random split safe for forecasting future readings?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The second attempt reads the archive without using more and more memory. ARIA confirms it is ready.

referenceInventory.summary: Reference: the full archive, buffers, and split policies

lessons.sourceBoundary: Read the archive without loading it all at once. The exercise currently uses a 16-row practice archive generated from row IDs.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: This is a generator/shuffle/split procedure, with no trained model. The fixture values stand in for sensor features and are not ship measurements. A full recording migration requires an explicit source contract.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Commander Mirza orders all sensor data normalized before the deep scan begins.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Feature scaling puts measurements on comparable scales. This can make a neural network easier to train.
recallQuestions: How can normalizing differently scaled features help training?
The readings have shape [4, 2], and the two column means have shape [2].
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The four sensor feeds now use a comparable scale. One archived reading still stands out.

referenceInventory.summary: Reference: choosing a scaler and the supplied neuron
Practice: a different scaler and reading

lessons.sourceBoundary: Fit feature statistics and scale later readings before a supplied fixed neuron. Current exercise data has four rows of temperature and signal strength, with no physical units.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: The neuron is supplied and frozen. Its score is not accuracy. Neither this two-feature fixture nor its model is the eight-feature network of module 2. Keep sample 7741’s unknown label and saved story decision unchanged.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Mirza needs a report for Earth Command in 6 hours. Farah proposes an LLM draft of 47 days of data, with time reserved to check its claims.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: An LLM generates a draft from instructions and context. Check its structure and claims before using it.
recallQuestions: Which workflow supports more trustworthy factual reports?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The model produces a first draft in minutes. Farah checks and corrects it. That saves time because she knows the data well enough to spot mistakes.

referenceInventory.summary: How a language model generates text

lessons.sourceBoundary: Parse the report assistant’s reply before passing it downstream. The exercise accepts a supplied mock API response.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: Valid JSON, allowed classification, and a bounded score establish structure only. No real API call occurs, and the score is no calibrated probability or validated scientific judgment.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Farah improves the prompt a little at a time and checks what changes in the draft. She treats it like debugging a search query, while still checking every claim.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Specific instructions and relevant context help define the task. Output also depends on the model, decoding settings and supplied evidence.
recallQuestions: What do the four prompt parts do, and what still needs checking?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The new template includes the sector catalogue. Farah tests both versions on held-out readings.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Build the prompt with relevant catalogue facts and the current reading. The result is the learner’s assembled text from supplied mission values.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: This exercise makes no model request. Do not fabricate before/after answers, compliance rates, or prompt-quality scores. A later real model test needs its own version and evaluated cases.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: The LLM has not seen DEEP SCAN's current signal data. Farah builds a RAG pipeline that finds matching database records and adds them to the prompt.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: RAG retrieves the relevant records first and hands them to the model, so answers can cite records you can inspect.
recallQuestions: Every number in a generated answer appears somewhere in retrieved records. Is the answer verified?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The database returns fourteen Band-7 records, but the model reports seventeen. Demir spends an hour checking earlier answers and building a claim checker.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Give the report inspectable records, then check numeric claims against exact citations. Current activities include both retrieval and structured-claim verification.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: The retriever uses a simple authored parser and keeps at most 20 rows. Matched records are not a token budget. Agreement with supplied records does not establish their truth or cover every claim in prose.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Farah needs a full scientific report for Earth Command: structured, cited, and professionally formatted. She builds a report generation pipeline using the LLM.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Report generation runs one prompt per section, each with its own data and its own check, and assembles only what passed.
recallQuestions: Why check each section and then check the whole report?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: One section fails its own validator with twenty-two minutes left before the window.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Assemble only reviewed sections for the relay. Current inputs contain fictional section text and earlier human validation decisions.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: The learner’s code formats and assembles supplied text. It does not review claims or call an LLM. A “validated” flag records a supplied decision, not automatic scientific approval.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Demir connects the full DEEP SCAN system. The classifier, autoencoder, and LSTM each process the same capture in their own format. The LLM uses their results to draft a report.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: A multi-model system divides the work between models. Pipeline code passes the right input to each model, checks the output, and moves it to the next step.
recallQuestions: Does passing the checks between stages prove the final prediction is correct?
Explain what you would investigate if a valid [0, 1] amplitude appears more than 3.47 standard deviations from a fixed mean of 0.52 and standard deviation of 0.15.
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The pipeline publishes a measured alert overnight. Its generated explanation waits for a human reviewer.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Connect classifier, detector, and alert-writing handoffs. The classifier runs a supplied model, while detector/writer callbacks are controlled.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: A plausible classification can be wrong. The callbacks do not run the full story autoencoder/LSTM/LLM system. Keep generated explanation separate from measured alert and human review.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: ARIA's rules cannot classify the unfamiliar signal. Farah starts with one neuron, a small function the crew can later train.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: A neuron multiplies each input by a weight, adds the results, then adds a bias. You will write that calculation here. The next lesson adds an activation function.
recallQuestions: Separate the three pieces of a neuron calculation.
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: One neuron separates the two calibration tones. Nazari watches it hold, then asks what sixty-four channels would cost.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Help Farah replace a handwritten rule with a weighted calculation. The artifact uses a fixed three-input arithmetic case.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: No training occurs in this exercise. A scalar result proves this calculation on these inputs, not classification ability or the source of the signal.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Nazari wants an alert rule. Farah first needs to check the activation that will connect the network's hidden layers.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: An activation function changes a neuron's score before passing it on. ReLU replaces negative values with zero. Sigmoid and tanh keep their outputs within fixed ranges.
recallQuestions: Why can one affine layer calculate the same output as a stack of affine dense layers?
Does an untrained sigmoid output of 0.99 establish a reliable 99% probability?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Farah has checked the hidden-layer activation. The alert threshold remains separate, and the model's scores still need evaluation.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Check hidden-layer activation before Nazari chooses an alert rule. Current probes supply negative, positive, and large pre-activation values.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: Activation and alert policy have different roles. Changing ReLU examples must not invent model evaluation or a deployment decision.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: One neuron can separate the two calibration tones. Nazari wants a network that can handle more complex patterns, and a count of the weights and biases it will need.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: A sequential network passes values through layers in order. Each layer changes the values before the next one reads them. Count its weights and biases to see how large the network is.
recallQuestions: Count the weights and biases in a dense layer.
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Nazari checks the count: 673 weights and biases. The network has its layers and still needs training.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Count the network’s weights and biases for Nazari. The exercise uses 16/8/1 layers with four input features, distinct from the story’s 32/16/1 model.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: The 16/8/1 practice stack is untrained. Do not display the story’s 673 count as this learner model’s count. Keep both model identities explicit.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: The first demo fails in front of the Commander. Demir supplied one flat reading, but the model expected rows. Farah tells him to fix it and run it again.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: A forward pass runs the input through the network to get an output. In this Sequential model, each layer passes its result to the next. Other network designs can have branches.
recallQuestions: The model input shape is [null, 8]. You have one example with eight features.
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The network returns scores. Demir has fixed the input shape. Now he needs to train the model.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Repair the batch-axis error in front of the commander. The exercise has two input features and a three-unit linear layer with random initial weights.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: A returned score verifies the forward calculation. Random initialization supplies no accuracy claim. Do not show a sigmoid probability scale for this linear output.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Commander Mirza gives the order: assemble the full signal classification network. Every component must work together.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Build the layers, choose their activations, and configure training with compile(). A new model can return predictions before training, but those scores are not evidence it has learned.
recallQuestions: You have created a model and called model.compile().
A dense layer maps three input features to 32 units.
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Demir has assembled and compiled DEEP SCAN. He saves its starting scores for comparison after training.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Assemble classifiers and compare their starting scores with a trained copy. The current exercise generates 120 eight-feature rehearsal rows and two independent models.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: The displayed 16-row excerpt comes from training. This is not held-out evaluation. The first three features are proxies and five are noise features. It does not continue the normalization model or its dataset.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: The crew lost the capture and missed the relay slot. Before trying to make DEEP SCAN smaller, they need to measure what it uses.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Profiling measures how much memory a model uses, how long predictions take, and how many parameters each layer has. Use those measurements to decide what to change.
recallQuestions: Separate what parameter profiling shows from what still needs measurement.
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The report shows weight-file size and prediction time separately. Nazari next wants to know the highest memory use while the model loads.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Measure the cost after the lost capture. Current output combines controlled-clock timing probes with actual parameter inventories.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: Controlled durations measure no device performance. Parameter bytes are not peak memory, and numTensors is not process memory. The missed capture and lost relay slot remain irreversible.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Nazari proposes storing the weights at lower precision. Uint8 would cut their stored size to a quarter of float32. She wants to see which predictions change.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Quantization stores weights in fewer bytes. Measure how it changes your model's predictions, memory use, and speed. Smaller files alone cannot tell you those results.
recallQuestions: What does quantization change, and what do you still need to measure?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The smaller build clears the engineering rig's load test. Nazari records its version beside the result and leaves the bridge-console check open.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Check what lower-precision weight storage changes. The exercise simulates uint8 kernel storage on a supplied synthetic multiclass model.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: The exercise does not pack a file or establish faster inference. Without labels, changed predictions indicate disagreement only. Biases remain float32, and constant-kernel behavior needs an explicit case.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Nazari sends Demir a five-sentence directive marked FOR REVIEW. It makes three assumptions. Help him check them before he signs off.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Magnitude pruning zeros the smallest weights. Measure how that changes predictions. A small weight is not necessarily unimportant.
recallQuestions: Why can zeroing 60% of weights leave an uncompressed dense weight file the same size?
Rare-class accuracy drops after magnitude pruning. Does that prove small weights represent rare patterns?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Pruning sets 60% of weights to zero. Accuracy falls from 94.2% to 91.8%, accounting for this module’s full 2.4-point loss. The 85 MB quantized bundle stays 85 MB. What drops is the download, to 42 MB gzipped. Demir's 80% experiment costs three hours.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Find which classes lose recall under requested pruning levels. The exercise trains a small synthetic classifier and re-scores actual variants on labeled examples.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: The existing view records aggregate curves. Actual share zeroed can differ from requested sparsity because tied weights remain. Restore original weights between trials and after failure. Do not claim sparse zeros guarantee smaller files or faster kernels.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Demir wants to reuse earlier predictions when an input repeats. Nazari asks him which model he timed.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: A valid cache hit can reuse a previous prediction and skip a model run. The hard part is deciding when two inputs count as the same.
recallQuestions: When does a cache save work, and when is a stored prediction still valid?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The next watch receives a cache policy and two threshold probes. Meanwhile, the smaller mission build frees the dashboard for the postponed sensor replays.

referenceInventory.summary: Compare cache reuse across request sequences

lessons.sourceBoundary: Reuse model outputs without hiding a changed decision. Current primary probe records a cache miss/hit. The incident audits version and age.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: Current artifact captures one repeated request, so a full trace needs new bounded capture. A version/TTL check cannot detect key collisions. Two rounded inputs can cross a threshold even with a valid cache version.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Nazari asks Demir to test another available backend and measure the fallback on the oldest console.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: WebGPU lets TensorFlow.js run supported tensor calculations on the GPU. Whether it is faster depends on the model, browser, and device.
recallQuestions: Why might WebGPU help, and how would you check whether it does?
A timer stops just after predict() and reports 0.4 ms. What is missing?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The dashboard survives the rehearsal. The crew records separate hit, miss and backend timings before approving the optimization stack.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Find a working console backend with fallback. The exercise supplies a controlled runtime whose preferred backends fail.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: This selects a working mock backend without measuring speed or GPU support. Browser workers remain under their current backend policy. Keep fallback success distinct from any claim that GPU is faster.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Farah finds a pattern across dozens of readings. The dashboard’s classifier sees only one reading at a time, so it cannot compare that sequence. She wants a model that can use earlier readings.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: A sequence is a list whose order matters. Rearranging the same readings can change the pattern they show.
recallQuestions: Does reversing the readings have the same effect as rearranging the features inside each reading?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Demir realizes the classifier is blind to temporal patterns because it reads one row at a time. The model processes each reading on its own. The model has no memory of what came before.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Give the classifier access to ordered context. Current result contains every input window/next-reading pair from a five-row synthetic stream.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: The target stays outside its input. This builds training pairs without training. Shapes alone cannot supply timestamps, units, or feature names.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Demir builds his first recurrent neural network: a network that maintains hidden state between time steps, using earlier readings as it processes the signal.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: An RNN updates a stored summary, called hidden state, after each reading. Training learns the weights used in that update.
recallQuestions: A simple RNN needs distant readings, but its loss stays near 0.693. What should you investigate?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Demir leaves the simple RNN training overnight. In the morning, its predictions still do not use the distant pattern.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Carry earlier information through hidden state. The exercise compares a JS recurrence with a one-unit layer and records synthetic state/derivative traces.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: The hand-chosen recurrence performs no training. Derivative decay illustrates one path and does not diagnose the overnight story model. Each call begins with fresh state.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: The simple RNN’s training signal fades before it reaches the distant anomaly pattern. Farah introduces an LSTM, which uses learned gates to control what it keeps.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: An LSTM uses learned gates to control how much of each stored value to keep, add and expose as output.
recallQuestions: How does an LSTM forget gate differ from expiring a stored value after a fixed time?
If the LSTM’s state resets between windows, what does it keep from training?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The LSTM trains on the archive’s first day and detects pulses in windows from three days later. Each window starts with fresh state, using the trained weights.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Check how gated state persists before using the longer-window model. The recorded artifact uses two synthetic state dimensions and fixed gate pre-activations.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: The exercise’s elementwise step is a teaching simplification. Keep its gate column ordering explicit. It does not establish learned long-range detection or state carried across days.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Demir creates overlapping windows, shuffles them and keeps every fifth pair for evaluation. The score is in the high nineties. Farah asks him to repeat it with 200 readings so he can check which readings landed in each set.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: A sliding window groups consecutive readings into one fixed-size input. Moving it forward creates the next input, which may share readings with the previous one.
recallQuestions: Explain why 97.4% accuracy on randomly split overlapping windows can be misleading for predicting a later period.
The target relationship is between readings 50 steps apart. The model resets state between windows.
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: With training and evaluation readings kept separate, the score falls from 97.4% to 60.6%. Demir also sends the dashboard its first complete 80-reading window.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Remove overlap leakage from the train/evaluation split. Current synthetic readings equal their own indices, with a cut before reading 8.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: This split is chronological by source reading. Do not carry the story’s 97.4%/60.6% scores into these returned arrays. Window labels here differ from the next-target task in sequences-matter.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Demir trains the LSTM to predict the next signal values. The bridge reports a promising short forecast. Farah asks for the error metric, its units and a baseline before trusting a longer one.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Sequence prediction estimates the next values from earlier readings. Check those estimates against later observations and a simple baseline.
recallQuestions: Why use a regression loss such as MSE for predicting the next sensor reading?
What does tf.tidy() release when the callback returns only numeric prediction values?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The forecast goes up on the main display with a 47-minute countdown, and nobody on the bridge leaves their station.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Use a trained forecaster’s outputs without claiming unsupported accuracy. Current result shows six recursive predictions from a synthetic training series.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: The current artifact supplies no future observed values. Do not add an observed curve, error percentage, or “better forecast” badge. This fixture’s three-feature scaler/model differs from earlier saved stages.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Farah reopens a capture from the first week. It shows the slow rise and fall she found when she arranged the readings into rows. She wants to see whether a frequency plot helps explain it.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Every signal has two representations: the time domain (amplitude over time) and the frequency domain (which frequencies are present). The full complex transform preserves the sampled information. A magnitude-only view drops phase.
recallQuestions: Why can a frequency representation make a weak periodic component easier to see?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Farah compares the same samples in time and frequency. A weak repeating component is easier to inspect in the spectrum.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Reinspect the same sampled capture in time and frequency. The exercise uses two synthetic two-second captures at 256 Hz.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: The supplied captures illustrate the crew’s task. A divergent bin requests inspection and identifies no physical source. Sample-value tolerance and raw FFT-magnitude cutoff use different scales.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: The overnight FFT has finished. Demir sees a peak in its output, but needs the frequency it represents. Farah helps him read the spectrum.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: The Fourier transform describes a signal using fixed sine and cosine waves. Its results tell you the strength and timing of each frequency component.
recallQuestions: The FFT uses 128 samples recorded at 128 samples per second.
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: A sharp peak at 73.4 Hz, and nothing in the catalog to explain it. 'That is not stellar background,' Farah says quietly.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Read the overnight peak as a frequency. The current exercise uses a synthetic one-second capture and excludes DC when selecting a winning bin.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: A one-second capture returns integer-Hz bin centers. It cannot establish the story’s exact 73.4 Hz. Off-bin leakage, neighboring tones, and ties need honest explanatory cases.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: One FFT shows the frequencies in one window of samples. Farah needs to see how those frequencies change over time, so she asks for a spectrogram.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: A spectrogram shows how frequency content changes over time, using one magnitude spectrum per window.
recallQuestions: What changes when you use a larger STFT window at the same sample rate?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The anomalous frequency appears in bursts, and the gap between pulses measures roughly 73.4 seconds.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Show Farah when frequency content changes. The current captured result is the 40 Hz bin across four non-overlapping frames of a synthetic one-second signal.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: Do not render a full heatmap from one bin. The exercise uses raw untapered slices, and its rFFT bin count differs from a library STFT with default Hann behavior. Frame timing must derive from sample rate and hop.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Demir adds FFT magnitudes to the classifier’s inputs. In the mission’s evaluation, accuracy rises from 78% to 87%. Farah asks him to explain what those extra inputs tell the model.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Feature engineering hands the model a better view of the same data: FFT magnitudes join the raw values as inputs, and may improve performance when those features help the task.
recallQuestions: Why might FFT magnitudes help a model that previously received only three summary features?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: DEEP SCAN 2.0 scores 87% on the mission’s evaluation. Its eight FFT inputs describe differences that the original three summary features could not capture.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Give DEEP SCAN ordered spectral features. The exercise uses a synthetic quarter-second capture at 256 Hz and retains a fixed frequency band.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: Unit-amplitude samples are not ADC counts. Keep raw magnitudes unscaled and ordered. The returned vector does not establish the story’s 78%-to-87% gain or compatibility with another model.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Demir’s FFT shows peaks where the recorder captured no separate tones. Farah checks for spectral leakage caused by cutting a finite window. She asks him to test a taper, which gives the edges less weight.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: A taper reduces distant spectral leakage by giving less weight to samples near the frame edges. It also broadens peaks and changes their heights.
recallQuestions: What tradeoff comes with applying a Hann window before an FFT?
What can go wrong if overlapping windows are randomly split into training and validation sets?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Hann windowing reduces distant leakage while broadening the main peak. The component near 73.4 Hz remains. Farah whispers: 'That is not noise. That is structure.'

lessons.sourceBoundary: Check distant leakage before calling extra peaks new tones. Current probes use a synthetic 128-sample, 10.5-cycle capture.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: Current output declares a table, so spectra need new bounded capture. The totals sum magnitudes, not energy. Tapering changes heights and peak width, with no guaranteed universal reduction factor.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: The network makes its first predictions. They're terrible. Dr. Farah needs a way to measure exactly how wrong they are.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: A loss function scores prediction errors with a chosen rule. Training tries to reduce that score.
recallQuestions: Match the loss to the outputs you have, then check one small squared-error calculation.
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Farah can now measure the prediction errors. Training will try to reduce that loss.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Help Farah measure wrong predictions. Current probes compare binary cross-entropy for fixed label/logit cases.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: The functions also assess MSE and BCE-form choice. Do not infer those skills from the BCE artifact alone. Logits and probabilities need distinct labels, and loss units follow the chosen function.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Knowing how wrong the network is isn't enough. Chief Nazari wants to know which direction to adjust.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Gradient descent uses the slope of the loss to choose a direction for changing the weights. A small enough step against that slope lowers the loss nearby.
recallQuestions: Loss explodes after a few steps. What is a reasonable next step?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Demir can now update one weight using its gradient. The other 672 still need updates.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Give Demir one inspectable weight update. The exercise uses scalar squared loss with weight 5 and learning rate 0.1.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: This scalar exercise trains no spacecraft classifier. The learning-rate experiment and exercise have distinct loss functions. Keep that distinction until an explicitly reviewed integration replaces both fixtures.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Demir can update one weight, but the network has 673. He tries changing them one at a time to measure their gradients.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Backpropagation computes gradients for every weight in one backward sweep, applying the chain rule from the loss back to the input.
recallQuestions: Separate gradient computation from weight updates.
Explain why estimating each parameter gradient with a separate forward pass becomes expensive as a model grows.
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: Backpropagation efficiently computes all 673 gradients in a single backward pass. The training engine is ready.

lessons.sourceBoundary: Replace Demir’s repeated forward calculations with automatic gradients. Probes compare numerical and automatic derivatives on supplied scalar-variable losses.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: Counts do not measure elapsed speed. Numerical approximation depends on epsilon. The small test is not a measured 673-weight training run.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Demir starts training the network on a hundred hand-picked signal examples.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: A training loop runs predictions, measures their errors, and updates the weights. It repeats those steps on the labeled examples.
recallQuestions: Read the validation stopping rule and decide what the loss curves can tell you.
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: The training run stops when validation loss stops improving, or when it reaches the epoch limit.

referenceInventory.summary: Reference: full training setup, checkpoints, and optimizer details

lessons.sourceBoundary: Stop a run when validation loss stops improving. The exercise generates 100 synthetic rows, uses validationSplit, and records real fit history.
lessons.limitsFromLessonMap: A valid run can reach the epoch limit. Current output samples up to 64 epochs and must not fabricate intermediate values. Validation loss is neither a final held-out score nor proof of the story outcome.

phaseEvidence.briefingNarrative: Training is complete. Mirza wants results on separate readings before allowing a supervised prototype test. A fleet release still needs the runtime and release checks in later modules.
phaseEvidence.conceptExplanation: Evaluation tests the model on data it has never seen. Compare held-out performance with a baseline and inspect the kinds of errors it makes.
recallQuestions: Explain what you would investigate before treating a 95% training versus 60% test accuracy gap as overfitting.
Keep train and validation membership fixed.
When can sensitivity and false-positive rate stay valid after anomalies become rarer?
phaseEvidence.consequenceNarrative: DEEP SCAN scores 94% on the crew's test readings. Mirza allows a supervised prototype test, but sample 7741 remains hard to classify.
